newsitem.title: SWITZERLAND: Swiss Re to buy Italy's Uniorias.
newsitem.headline: Swiss Re to buy Italy's Uniorias.

text.p: Swiss Reinsurance Co signed an agreement to acquire Italy's Unione Italiana di Riassicurazione SpA (Uniorias) and insurance analysts hailed the deal based on its price and structure.
Swiss Re said it was buying Uniorias from Instituto Nazionale delle Assicurazoni SpA (INA) for an expected price of 500 million Swiss francs.
It is based on the adjusted net asset value of Uniorias as of December 31, 1996 plus a payment for goodwill of 200 billion lire, mostly for the value of the in-force life business of Uniorias.
"It's a reasonable amount of money to spend to become the number one re-insurer in Italy," one London analyst said.
Uniorias is the leading reinsurer in the Italian market.
The arrangement is structured in stages and permits Swiss Re to take on the Rome-based company's reinsurance portfolio while leaving behind real estate.

"They (Swiss Re) have said they do not want to become a real estate owner in Italy so I think this was a prerequisite for taking over Uniorias," said Thomas Della Putta, real estate analyst at Pictet & Cie.
Swiss Re said the arrangement calls for it to acquire 49 percent of Uniorias early in 1997.
The business will subsequently be restructured to separate reinsurance from the excess real estate and securities.
The arrangement also provides for the retrocession of certain exisiting business portfolios of Uniorias to Assitalia.
Following this, Swiss Re will acquire the balance of 51 percent of Unioras at the end of 1997.
The deal is in line with the prevailing strategy at Swiss Re to expand through selective acquisition.

"The reason they make acquisitions is because it is cheaper for them to buy a business and improve on it than to grow internally...their cost of capital is low because they are so diversified," one London analyst said.
Swiss Re in August bought Mercantile and General Re, Britain's oldest and largest reinsurance firm, from Britain's Prudential Corp for around 3.15 billion Swiss francs in cash.

Pictet's Della Putta said the deal looked interesting both from a strategic and a price point of view even considering the fact that there is only limited information at hand on the Italian company's profitability.
"They (Swiss Re) have clear financial targets on every transaction. Any new risk business would have to have the same target rates as the existing portfolio," he said.
"As far as can be judged now it (the acquisition) would not be dilutive for Swiss Re," he added.
Beat Alpiger of Bank Julius Baer said the Uniorias life re-insurance business should hold good potential for Swiss Re in the Italian market, which has a seven to nine percent growth rate.
Uniorias writes non-life, which accounts for 78 percent of its business and life, which makes up the remaining 22 percent.
However, analysts split over Swiss Re's announcement it had acquired 0.75 percent of INA's share capital on the Milan Stock Exchange.
"Why should they commit capital to a primary insurer when they (Swiss Re) are a reinsurer?" the London analyst asked.
But Pictet's Della Putta said this link to INA could develop into good business in the longer term, depending on how it develops.
Swiss Re's share price was up 14 Swiss francs to 1,405 at 1230 GMT.
